title: Samkhya (the 24 principles
hook: a film plays in a dark room, and someone is watching it: Samkhya's first two

segments.voice: Yesterday a new lens opened: Samkhya, which starts with pain and counts twenty-four principles, plus one standing outside the count. What pain did you sort? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-two.

A film is playing on a laptop in a dark room. A storm, a car chase, a wedding, a funeral. The light on the wall keeps changing color. On the couch, somebody is watching. The storm doesn't get them wet. The funeral doesn't bury them. And yet without them, nobody would be seeing any of it. So there are two things in that room: everything that shows up on the screen, and the one it shows up for. Samkhya starts its whole count right there, with two that never blend into each other. Today we meet them by name.
screen: `A FILM IN A DARK ROOM.` → `SOMEONE IS WATCHING.` → `TWO THAT NEVER BLEND.`

segments.voice: The first is prakriti. The Samkhya Karika, the book of verses we opened yesterday, calls it the root, and says the root is not itself made by anything. Everything else unfolds out of it. Mountains and rivers, yes. Your body, yes. But here's the surprise: your senses, your mind, your thoughts and even your sense of being an I all sit on prakriti's side of the line. In Samkhya, thinking is part of nature. A worry is as much a thing in the world as a cloud. The second is purusha. The Karika describes it in a short string of words: a witness, a seer, neutral, standing apart, not the one doing anything. Purusha doesn't think the thoughts. It's the one they appear in front of. And the Karika says there isn't just one purusha. It reasons this way: people are born separately, die separately, and have their own senses, so each has a purusha of their own. Other schools see this point differently. Advaita Vedanta, one of the Vedanta schools we'll meet later, reads the self as one. Samkhya keeps many, and the schools are allowed to disagree. So what does this change in a day? It moves a line most of us draw without looking. A wave of irritation, a plan for dinner, a memory from school: Samkhya would put all of them on the screen. Something in you is watching the film. Samkhya's name for that something is purusha.
screen: `PRAKRITI: THE ROOT, NOT MADE.` · `THOUGHTS SIT ON NATURE'S SIDE.` · `PURUSHA: THE WITNESS.` · `MANY WITNESSES, NOT ONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the film play for two minutes. Sit, and let your breath settle. Then let things show up. A sound from the street. An itch. A thought about tomorrow. Each time something appears, you don't have to push it away or follow it. Just note, quietly, seen. Then wait for the next thing. Sounds, feelings and thoughts all go on the same screen. If you pray, you can let a prayer be one more thing that shows up, and is seen. The bell holds the time.
Samkhya. A school of thought that counts out the world, and starts with two: purusha, the one who sees, and prakriti, everything seen.
Your line: Samkhya, the twenty-four principles. Today, once, when a mood rolls in, try calling it something on the screen, and notice who is watching it. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: Samkhya is studied through the Samkhya Karika and its commentaries, and its map of purusha and prakriti is taught alongside the Yoga Sutras, which build on it.

fork.setup: you're studying with a Samkhya teacher. she asks: your worry about tomorrow, which side of the line does it sit on?
fork.reveal: in Samkhya, thoughts and worries are part of prakriti, as much in the world as a cloud. purusha is the one they appear to.

original.note: Sanskrit: in Samkhya, the witness, the seer that stands apart from everything seen.

trapdoor: what you thought: purusha is the soul doing the thinking.
what it means: in Samkhya, purusha only witnesses. the thinking itself is on prakriti's side.
what a scholar hears: Samkhya Karika 19 calls purusha a witness, neutral, a seer, not an agent, and verse 18 argues there are many of them.
